strengths: Well-motivated and timely consolidation of a fragmented but rapidly growing area (86% of the 134 surveyed papers post-2023), with a clear unifying framing of citation, attribution, and quotation as one paradigm ('evidence-based text generation')

Methodologically rigorous systematic mapping study: explicit research questions, documented search string, nine databases, explicit inclusion criteria, dual independent screening, and a documented categorization scheme adapted from established guidelines (Petersen et al., 2008; Schneider et al., 2022)

Substantial and reusable resource: taxonomy across four dimensions (attribution approach, LLM integration, citation characteristics, task), 300 evaluation metrics organized by seven dimensions and six methods, 231 datasets, 17 frameworks, and 11 benchmarks, with an annotated dataset released in a public Git repository supporting reproducibility

The extension of prior attribution taxonomies (adding in-generation and in-context to post-retrieval/post-generation; splitting parametric attribution into pure LLM, model-centric, and data-centric) is a genuine conceptual contribution beyond prior surveys

The evaluation section (Section 6) and Figure 7 provide genuinely useful practical guidance, including complementary metric clusters and an honest diagnosis of evaluation fragmentation (only two frameworks/benchmarks reused)
Discussion identifies concrete, well-supported open problems (parametric attribution gap, evaluation standardization, explainable citation behavior) grounded in the collected statistics
weaknesses: The analysis is largely descriptive (counting papers per category) rather than analytical; the synthesis offers limited critical assessment of method quality, contradictory findings, or comparative insights across the surveyed approaches, which limits its value beyond a well-organized catalog

No inter-annotator agreement or reliability statistics are reported for the two-annotator categorization of 134 papers across many multi-valued dimensions, which weakens confidence in the reported distribution statistics

The search strategy (matching title/abstract only, on a fixed term list) likely misses relevant work that does not use 'citation', 'attribution', or 'quote' in title/abstract (e.g., traceability, grounded generation, provenance); potential recall loss is not quantified or discussed as a threat to validity
Search cutoff of February 2025 with only 10 papers from 2025 means the landscape analysis will age quickly, and the projection of 'continued growth' is speculative

Presentation issues: Figure 7 is dense and difficult to parse at print resolution; minor text errors (e.g., 'the revised text y retains from the original output x', 'categorized into seven dimensions and six method') suggest a needed copy-editing pass

Some claims feel under-supported or anecdotal, e.g., the assertion that parametric approaches 'are often unable to produce multiple citations due to architectural constraints' is stated without citation or evidence

The RQs are broad and the answers remain at a surface level; deeper questions (which approach families actually perform better, how metrics correlate, known limitations of NLI-based attribution metrics) are not systematically addressed

strengths: Follows a structured, systematic mapping methodology (Petersen et al., 2008) with explicit research questions, a documented search string, nine literature databases, stated inclusion criteria, and dual-screening, which makes the survey procedure transparent.

Timely and relevant topic: evidence-based text generation (citations, attribution, quotations) is an active and fragmented area, and the paper correctly identifies the terminology inconsistency and evaluation-fragmentation problems.

Substantial empirical coverage: 134 papers, 300 metrics, 17 frameworks, 231 datasets, and 11 benchmarks, with the annotated dataset made available in a public Git repository, supporting reproducibility.

The taxonomy makes some genuinely useful distinctions, e.g., extending the Li et al. (2023) post-retrieval/post-generation split with in-generation and in-context attribution, and decomposing parametric attribution into pure-LLM, model-centric, and data-centric types.

The evaluation section (Section 6, Figure 7) usefully maps metrics onto evaluation methods and dimensions, and the observation that only two frameworks/benchmarks are reused is a well-supported and actionable finding.
weaknesses: The search string (("large language model" OR "llm") AND ("citation" OR "attribution" OR "quote")) likely misses a substantial portion of the relevant literature. Key community terms such as "grounded (text) generation", "verifiable generation", "traceable", and "groundedness" are excluded, raising doubts about the claimed comprehensiveness despite 805 candidates being screened.

No inter-annotator agreement is reported. With two authors independently screening titles/abstracts and then annotating 134 papers across many subjective dimensions (e.g., 'approach' vs. 'resource', attribution subtype), agreement statistics (Cohen's kappa) are essential for reproducibility and credibility, but are absent.

Much of the taxonomy and categorization is inherited rather than novel: the parametric/non-parametric split and post-retrieval/post-generation categories come directly from Huang and Chang (2024) and Li et al. (2023). The contribution is incremental on top of these works, and the paper's claim of being 'the first comprehensive survey' is asserted more than demonstrated against these overlapping surveys.

The synthesis is largely descriptive frequency counting. Sections 4–6 mostly report how many papers do X (e.g., 58% zero-shot, 96% text modality, 71% QA), without deep critical analysis of why the field is fragmented, how approaches compare, or what the identified gaps imply methodologically.

The analysis reveals sparse categories but the paper does not adjust its framing accordingly: e.g., only seven parametric-attribution studies and a handful of non-textual citation modalities, so several taxonomy branches and associated percentages rest on very few papers and risk over-interpretation.

The Discussion (Section 7) is thin. The three identified challenges (parametric attribution, evaluation standards, explainable citations) are reasonable but superficially argued, and the 'Explainable Citations' direction in particular lacks supporting evidence from the reviewed corpus (no analysis of citation-bias studies is provided).

Several claims lack evidence or explanation: e.g., the assertion that 'parametric approaches are often unable to produce multiple citations due to architectural constraints' is stated without citation or analysis; the abstract's 75%/62%/13% terminology statistics are never clearly defined or reconciled with the taxonomy.

Figure 7 is dense and hard to parse, and the relationship between the 300 metrics, the seven dimensions, and the six methods is only partially conveyed; the claim of '300 distinct metrics' would benefit from consolidation, since many are trivial variants (e.g., precision/recall/F1 instantiations).

The survey will age quickly: the February 2025 cutoff leaves the field's fastest-growing period (2025) largely uncovered, which, combined with the descriptive nature of the content, limits lasting value unless the released repository is maintained and updated.

No empirical component or meta-analysis: the survey does not, for example, re-evaluate the identified benchmarks, compare metric behaviors, or validate its proposed 'complementary metric clusters' — opportunities that would have elevated the contribution beyond a literature count.

strengths: Systematic and transparent methodology: the paper follows established systematic mapping guidelines (Petersen et al., 2008), reports the search string, queried databases, inclusion criteria, screening process, and contribution-type scheme, which supports reproducibility of the literature collection process.

Timely and useful resource: covering 134 papers, 300 evaluation metrics, 17 frameworks, 231 datasets, and 11 benchmarks with a public annotated dataset is a genuinely valuable reference for a fast-moving and fragmented research area; 86% of the covered work post-dates prior surveys, justifying the effort.

The taxonomy is well-organized and clearly presented (attribution approach, LLM integration, citation characteristics, task), and the paper is candid about where it extends prior categorizations (e.g., adding in-generation and in-context attribution to the post-retrieval/post-generation dichotomy).

The evaluation section is arguably the strongest part: mapping 300 metrics into six evaluation methods and seven dimensions, identifying complementary metric clusters, and highlighting the severe lack of standardization (only two frameworks/benchmarks reused) provides actionable insight for the community.

The discussion goes beyond description by identifying concrete gaps (parametric attribution underexplored, no standardized evaluation, unexplained citation behavior) with clear future-work directions.
Clear writing and well-structured figures and tables; the distinction between frameworks and benchmarks is sensibly defined and applied consistently in the appendix tables.
weaknesses: No inter-annotator agreement or reliability statistics are reported. The paper states annotations were split between the first two authors with 'regular reviews,' but without Cohen's kappa or a comparable measure, the consistency of the 134-paper categorization across ~10 dimensions cannot be assessed, which weakens the soundness of the reported distributions.

The search strategy has potential coverage gaps that are not discussed: the string requires 'citation', 'attribution', or 'quote' in title/abstract, which may miss relevant work using 'quotation', 'grounding', 'traceability', 'verifiable generation', or 'evidence-based' terminology—ironically reinforcing the terminology fragmentation the paper itself identifies. The matching semantics (exact word vs. substring, plural forms) are also unspecified.

Several headline counts are ambiguous due to multi-label assignment: e.g., 126 non-parametric + 25 parametric approaches exceed 134 papers, and Figure 5 sums to 150; the reader must infer that papers receive multiple labels, and the paper does not clearly state the annotation rules for such cases.

The analysis is largely descriptive (frequency counts per year, per category); there is little deeper synthesis, e.g., no critical assessment of which method families perform better under which evaluation conditions, no correlation of trends (e.g., prompting vs. training adoption over time), and the extrapolation of 2025 growth is speculative.

Novelty of the taxonomy is incremental: it explicitly builds on Huang and Chang (2024) and Li et al. (2023), and some dimensions (e.g., citation style, evidence level) overlap with prior attribution surveys, so the 'first comprehensive survey' claim is only partially differentiated and should be stated more carefully.

Some classifications and claims are debatable or thinly supported: e.g., the assertion that 'parametric approaches are often unable to produce multiple citations due to architectural constraints' is not substantiated; the 71% QA share partly reflects how tasks were delineated rather than an intrinsic property of the field.
The February 2025 cutoff means the survey will age quickly in a field where it reports 6.6-fold annual growth; a maintenance/plan for updating the repository is not discussed.

Minor issues: Figure 7 is dense and hard to parse in its printed form; the related-work distinction from RAG surveys (Gao et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2024) could be sharper since post-retrieval attribution substantially overlaps with attributed RAG.

strengths: Fills a genuine gap: this appears to be the first systematic mapping study (PRISMA protocol) dedicated to evidence-based text generation with LLMs, consolidating a highly fragmented field that existing surveys only cover partially (RAG, hallucination, attribution).

Rigorous and transparent methodology: documented search strings, nine databases, explicit inclusion criteria, PRISMA flow diagram, sensitivity analysis of the search strategy, and measured inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's α) for both screening and taxonomy annotation.

Substantial, reusable contribution: 134 annotated papers, 300 evaluation metrics classified by seven dimensions and six methods, 19 frameworks, 11 benchmarks, and 231 datasets, with a public annotated dataset under a BSD license supporting reproducibility and future work.

The proposed multidimensional (facetted) taxonomy (attribution approach, citation characteristics, task) is well motivated and finer-grained than prior categorizations, e.g., extending parametric attribution into pure/model-centric/data-centric and adding in-generation and in-context attribution classes.

The evaluation guidelines (Table 1) distinguishing core vs. contextual dimensions are a concrete, actionable output beyond a descriptive review, and the per-dimension 'Takeaways' boxes make the survey digestible.
Well organized and clearly written; the extensive appendices (per-task analyses, temporal trends, metric tables) support the main text without overloading it.
weaknesses: The analyses are largely descriptive/distributional (counts and percentages); while trends are well documented, the paper offers limited deeper synthesis (e.g., little quantitative or qualitative comparison of why certain paradigms succeed or fail), which limits scientific novelty beyond consolidation.

Inter-annotator agreement of α = 1.0 (perfect agreement) on 50 screening studies is suspicious and weakens credibility of the annotation validation; the annotation sample sizes (30–50 papers) are small.

Search matched only title and abstract with a single keyword string; the sensitivity analysis (4% additional studies) mitigates this, but recall risk in a fast-moving field with inconsistent terminology remains, and the data cut-off (February 2025) means the survey will age quickly.
The data-availability link in Appendix A is an incomplete placeholder (https://github.com/), undermining verifiability of the central resource claim in its current form.
Several figures are dense and hard to read (e.g., Figure 4 with many small metric boxes, Figure 7's multi-class stacked bars), which reduces usability despite the richness of the content.

Some takeaways reiterate well-known observations (e.g., RAG/post-retrieval dominance, text-centric evidence, QA dominating tasks) without strong new insight; the '300 metrics' count inflates the contribution somewhat given many are task-specific variants.

strengths: Rigorous and transparent survey methodology: PRISMA-compliant screening (1,040 records -> 134 included), pre-registered-style inclusion criteria, sensitivity analysis with an expanded search string (identifying only 4% additional studies), and inter-annotator agreement measured with Krippendorff's alpha (mostly 0.77-1.00) across taxonomy dimensions.

Comprehensive and well-organized synthesis: a facetted, multi-label taxonomy (attribution approach, citation characteristics, task), a systematic catalog of 300 evaluation metrics across 7 dimensions and 6 methods, plus frameworks, benchmarks, and datasets, with temporal trend and per-task analyses in extensive appendices.

Actionable contribution beyond description: the core vs. contextual evaluation-dimension guidelines (Table 1) and the comparative metric table with measured aspects and limitations (Table 9) provide concrete practical value for researchers selecting evaluation protocols.

The unified framing of attribution/citation/quotation under 'evidence-based text generation' genuinely clarifies fragmented terminology, and per-dimension 'Takeaways' boxes make the synthesis digestible.
Annotated dataset of all 134 papers promised under a permissive license supports reproducibility and future research.
weaknesses: The novelty claim ('first survey dedicated to this paradigm') is weakened by the authors' own corpus: Zhang et al. (2023a) 'When large language models meet citation' is itself a survey of this space, and Li et al. (2023a) covers LLM attribution; the related-work section dismisses these without adequately differentiating the actual incremental contribution (mainly the post-2023 coverage and the evaluation-metrics catalog).

The analysis is largely descriptive counting. Many takeaways restate well-known facts (text dominates citations at 96%, QA dominates tasks, prompting dominates at 78%, ALCE is the only reused framework) without deeper critical synthesis, e.g., why fragmentation persists or comparative assessment of which methods actually work.

Trend claims are over-interpreted from very small cell counts (e.g., token-level evidence n=2, in-generation attribution n=5, 2025 n=5 papers, fact verification n=3), and statements like 'anticipated continued growth' extrapolate from a truncated sample.

Reproducibility is currently compromised: the repository URL appears as an incomplete placeholder ('https://github.com/') in both the footnote and Appendix A, so the claimed public dataset cannot be located as submitted.

Moderate annotation reliability for a key dimension (contribution type alpha = 0.73), and agreement could not be computed for the parametric attribution dimension at all; subjective multi-label categorization is only partially mitigated.

The critical evaluation of metrics is thin in the main text; limitations of the dominant metrics (NLI-based citation precision/recall, ROUGE/BERTScore as attribution proxies) are catalogued rather than analyzed, e.g., no discussion of known failure modes or correlation studies between metric families.
Coverage ends February 2025, so a substantial fraction of the field (already growing 3.4x/year by their own numbers) will be missing at publication; the paper will age quickly.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: evidence-based text generation with LLMs (citations, attribution, quotation) is a rapidly growing but fragmented area, and this appears to be the first survey dedicated to the full paradigm rather than isolated aspects such as RAG or hallucination.

Methodologically rigorous for a survey: PRISMA-based systematic mapping study, documented search strings, nine databases, explicit inclusion criteria, inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha reported per dimension), and a sensitivity analysis with an expanded term set that quantifies recall risk (only 4% additional relevant papers).

Substantial and reusable resources: 134 annotated papers, 300 evaluation metrics organized by method and dimension, 19 frameworks, 11 benchmarks, and 231 datasets, with a public repository and a large appendix (Table 7 provides full per-paper annotation).

The taxonomy is well-motivated (facetted classification with multi-label assignment) and genuinely illuminating, e.g., revealing that in-generation attribution (4%) and non-textual evidence modalities remain underexplored, and that only two evaluation frameworks (ALCE, G-Eval) are reused across studies.

Practical value beyond description: Table 1's core-vs-contextual evaluation guidelines and Table 9's metric limitations table provide actionable guidance for future researchers, and the four future directions (parametric/hybrid attribution, evaluation standards, explainable citations, multimodal evidence) are grounded in the quantitative findings.
Clear writing with consistent takeaways boxes per dimension; trends analysis over time (quarterly granularity) adds analytic depth beyond a static snapshot.
weaknesses: Literature coverage relies on a restrictive single search string ('large language model' OR 'llm') AND ('citation' OR 'attribution' OR 'quote') matched against title/abstract. The sensitivity analysis mitigates this partially, but studies using terms like 'verifiable generation', 'grounded answers', or 'provenance' in titles/abstracts without the primary keywords may still be missed; five relevant papers were found only through the sensitivity search yet were excluded from the corpus, which is debatable.

The search cutoff is February 2025, so the survey will be quickly dated given the field's growth trajectory; the paper itself acknowledges this, but it limits long-term utility and the 2025 analysis (only five papers) is not interpretable.

Much of the contribution is descriptive mapping rather than critical synthesis; while statistics on distributions and trends are useful, deeper comparative analysis of why certain paradigms dominate, or what trade-offs different approaches embody, is thinner (though Section 5.2 and Appendix D partially compensate).

Some reporting fragility: the dataset URL is truncated/incomplete in the manuscript ('https://github.com/'), undermining the reproducibility claim as presented; readers cannot verify the annotated dataset from the submission itself.

Perfect inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha = 1.0) on the 50-paper inclusion sample is reported; while possible, such a result warrants more discussion of the sample and process, as it can suggest the ambiguity of the inclusion criteria was underestimated or the sample too small/easy.

Several taxonomy boundaries are judgment calls that could affect counts (e.g., classifying PURR as post-retrieval despite its hybrid nature; 'in-context' attribution being partly an evaluation setting rather than a method), and these choices could have been stress-tested more explicitly.

Claims of completeness ('first survey dedicated to this paradigm') should be treated with care given concurrent survey activity in attribution/RAG-adjacent areas, though the paper's differentiation from Li et al. (2023a) and Huang and Chang (2024) is reasonably argued.
